title: An Impossible Choice: When Schools Make Families Choose Education or Safety
author: First Fish Chronicles
summary: In this open letter to Seattle Public Schools leadership, a parent writing as First Fish Chronicles explains why her family is reluctantly accepting a district-issued 1:1 Chromebook for her daughter's 9th grade year after successfully declining one for two years of middle school. The letter argues that because so much of the district's curriculum, grading, and homework is now only accessible through the device, opting out has become equivalent to excluding her daughter from a comparable education - an 'impossible choice' between safety/privacy and participation. Rather than simply refusing the device, the author lays out specific, actionable requests: that the district disable all GenAI features (naming Microsoft CoPilot, Canva, ChatGPT, Google products, and MagicSchoolAI explicitly), block YouTube, Pinterest, and social and gaming platforms, and stop treating the blanket 'Student Use Agreement' checkbox as legally meaningful informed consent. The author is explicit that she does not consent to the data collection and privacy risks involved but is checking the box anyway because district policy does not permit families to provide or control an alternative device. She shares the letter as a template other parents can adapt when raising similar concerns with their own districts.
points: The letter documents a specific, concrete request: that Seattle Public Schools disable GenAI features (naming Microsoft CoPilot, Canva, ChatGPT, Google products, and MagicSchoolAI) and block YouTube, Pinterest, and social/gaming platforms on the district-issued device, rather than simply refusing the device outright.

The author argues the district's blanket 'Student Use Agreement' checkbox does not constitute meaningful, informed consent, because it bundles dozens of distinct apps and privacy policies into a single sign-off.

The family's core complaint is structural: after successfully avoiding a 1:1 device for two years, the shift to high school made curriculum and grading effectively device-dependent, eliminating any real opt-out.

The letter frames this as a broader pattern — families forced to choose between their child's data privacy/safety and their participation in a standard education — and offers itself as a template for other parents to adapt.
quotes: It was our intention to send a letter informing the district of our continued plan to decline the use of the district-issued internet-connected Chromebook this fall for our daughter as she enters the 9th grade.

We are deeply concerned about the implications of this, not just on the impact of screen-based technology on her (and other students' learning), but because we believe that the district is forcing students to choose between their health and privacy or an education.

We do not consent to the use of any AI-enabled products, especially GenAI, whether that is via a stand-alone app, platform, or website, or within an existing EdTech product, tool, or curricula that contains embedded GenAI components, such as Microsoft CoPilot, Canva, ChatGPT, Google products, or MagicSchoolAI.

To login to a school-issued device, students are required to sign a blanket "Student Use Agreement." As there are many unique apps and platforms contained within the district devices, unless each privacy policy is presented to parents individually to obtain meaningful and informed consent, this "checkbox" does not suffice as legally binding consent.

We have reached a point in our daughter's educational journey in Seattle Public Schools where attempting to decline the 1:1 means accepting an education that would be sufficiently different from her peers.

We are accepting the laptop solely because we do not feel we have any choice in the matter, and even if we wanted her to have a laptop, SPS policy does not allow us to personally provide her with a device that we could control or monitor.
